context_blurb:
Flip a switch, and a lamp lights at once. Electricity reaches it through wires, but only along a path that runs all the way round and back again, like a toy train on a closed loop of track. Learn how that path works, and you can explain a flashlight or a doorbell, and stay safe near electricity.

Electricity flows only round a complete loop with no gaps. It leaves one end of a battery, runs along a wire and through a bulb, then comes home along another wire to the battery's other end. That whole path, out and back, is called a circuit. The electricity moving round it is the current, and copper wire is a conductor, a material that lets electricity flow. Every circuit also needs a battery, or some other source of energy, to push the electricity round. The wires only give it a path, so a buzzer in a perfect loop of copper wire stays silent until a battery joins the loop.

Try a puzzle with one battery, one bulb and one wire. Join the battery's top to the bulb's metal base with the wire, and let nothing else touch. The bulb stays dark. The electricity has no path back to the battery, so none flows at all. Nothing gets used up, and no switch is needed to start it. Now keep the wire on the side of the bulb's base and press the tip of the base against the battery's bottom end. The loop is complete, and the bulb lights.

A switch is a gate in the loop. Switch a flashlight on, and two metal parts inside the switch touch: metal touching metal closes the circuit, so electricity can cross. Switch it off, and the parts move apart, leaving a gap: the circuit is open, and nothing flows. These words run opposite to a door's. An open door lets people through, but an open switch lets no electricity through.

A gap anywhere in a single loop stops the electricity all the way round. Suppose the wire running back from a glowing bulb slips off the battery. The bulb goes out at once, even though the gap is after the bulb. No electricity waits in the wire to keep it glowing. That is also why a switch works wherever it sits in the loop.

The metal inside a lamp's cord, and in the wiring hidden in a house's walls, is copper. Copper carries electricity better than every metal except silver, which costs many times as much, and copper bends round corners without cracking. Around the copper is a coat of plastic. Plastic is an insulator, a material that does not let electricity pass. The coat keeps the current inside the metal and away from a person's hand on the cord. A cord with cracked plastic and bare wire showing is dangerous to touch.

Metals are not the only conductors. Tap water is not pure: it carries dissolved minerals. Those minerals let tap water pass electricity through it, though perfectly pure water barely lets any through. Water makes no electricity of its own, but it carries any that reaches it. So keep anything with a plug away from a bath, a sink or a pool, and dry wet hands before you touch a switch.

The same rule explains birds on power lines. The thick lines strung between tall towers are bare metal, with no plastic coat. A small bird perched on a single line touches nothing else, so the electricity has no path through its body, and almost none flows through it. But if a big bird's wings or feet touch two lines at once, its body completes a loop between them, like a bulb set between a battery's two ends, and electricity rushes through it. Touching a line and a tower at once is just as dangerous.
